summary: A 60-ft steel fire tower on Kittatinny Mountain near Catfish Pond, opened in 1922, rebuilt in 1993 and repainted in 2022; staffed in fire weather and reached on foot.

facts.design: 7 x 7 ft cab on a 60-ft Aermotor LS-40 steel tower

staffing.status: staffed sometimes, during elevated fire danger; full-time observer post vacant

access.note: Reached on foot along the Appalachian Trail; a fire road from Millbrook Road joins the route. A 2018 visit report saw no trail signage on the Appalachian Trail.

visit.trail_note: About a 2-mile hike, per a 2018 visit report. A 2018 report found no trail signage on the Appalachian Trail in either direction.

facts.agency: New Jersey Forest Fire Service (tower within Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area)

events.note: Steel tower opened near Catfish Pond in July 1922; the NHLR says it replaced an earlier wooden tower.
State FY1923 report: a connecting telephone line of about eight miles of new line was built to the tower.
Norman Maring employed as watchman, per the Easton Free Press in August 1924. First named staffer in the sources read; earlier staffing was not checked.
The 7 x 7 ft cab was rebuilt on the existing 60-ft Aermotor LS-40 tower.
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register, December 15, 1997.
Repainted in May 2022 for the 100th anniversary; interior repairs were planned.

evidence.supports: Located on the Appalachian Trail inside the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area; built 1922 replacing a wooden tower.
evidence.quote: Located on the Appalachian Trail in the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area, Catfish Fire Tower was constructed in 1922, replacing a wooden tower.

evidence.supports: The cab was rebuilt in 1993 on the 60-ft Aermotor LS-40 tower.
evidence.quote: In 1993 the 7’ x 7’ cab was rebuilt on this 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower.

evidence.supports: Repainted in May 2022 for the 100th anniversary.
evidence.quote: The tower was repainted in May 2022, with other repairs planned, in recognition of its 100th anniversary.

evidence.supports: Registered on the NHLR on December 15, 1997.
evidence.quote: Date Registered December 15, 1997

evidence.supports: A fire road is combined with access to the tower from Millbrook Road.
evidence.quote: A fire road is combined with access to the tower on the Appalachian Trail from Millbrook Road.

evidence.supports: Staffed during elevated fire danger by a Forest Fire Observer.
evidence.quote: The tower is staffed during periods of elevated fire danger (moderate +) or whenever the forest is dry enough to burn, by a Forest Fire Observer.

evidence.supports: Full-time observer post vacant; part-time observer available.
evidence.quote: The full time Forest Fire Observer position for this tower is currently vacant, however a steady part-time Fire Observer is available for this station.

evidence.supports: 2018 visit found no staff present; tower still appears in commission.
evidence.quote: No staff were present, however, the tower does appear to still be in commission.

evidence.supports: A second 2018 visit found a person in the tower during the day.
evidence.quote: When I went there during the day there was a guy in the tower.

evidence.supports: A 2018 visitor described the hike as about two miles.
evidence.quote: About a 2 mile hike to the tower, nice and easy.

evidence.supports: 2018 visit noted warped angle iron on landings; steel otherwise sound.
evidence.quote: Warped angle iron on first and fifth Landings, but otherwise steel seems to be in good structural condition.

evidence.supports: Tower painted in May 2022 for its 100th anniversary.
evidence.quote: The tower was painted in May of 2022 for its 100th anniversary.

evidence.supports: 2018 visit found no trail signage on the Appalachian Trail in either direction.
evidence.quote: there does not appear to be any signage

evidence.supports: Height 60 feet (18 m); elevation 1,555 feet.
evidence.quote: Catfish Station 1,555 feet (474 m) 60 feet (18 m)

evidence.supports: Tower on Kittatinny Mountain, about 7 miles west of Blairstown (state FY1923 report).
evidence.quote: On Kittatinny Mountain at a point about 7 miles west of Blairstown, Warren County, a 60 foot steel tower and a connecting telephone line have been completed.

evidence.supports: June 1922 announcement: the new steel tower on Blue Mountain near the Catfish pond.
evidence.quote: It has been decided to locate the new steel fire tower on the summit of the Blue Mountain half way between the Millbrook road and the Catfish pond.

evidence.supports: Opened in July 1922 as a 60-foot steel tower of the State Forest Fire Service.
evidence.quote: with the opening of a new 60-foot steel tower by the State Forest Fire Service

evidence.supports: Tower open to the public, per the 1922 press.
evidence.quote: The tower, like the other fire towers in New jersey, is open to the public.

evidence.supports: Asbury Park Press, July 1922: about five miles west of Blairstown.
evidence.quote: It is sixty feet high and situated about five miles west of Blairstown on the Blairstown-Millbrook road.

evidence.supports: Telephone line opened new territory along its route.
evidence.quote: The telephone line necessary to connect the tower site with the blairstown exchange has opened up a new territory along its route

evidence.supports: State FY1923 report: 8-mile telephone connection, all new line.
evidence.quote: The 8-mile telephone connection is all new line

evidence.supports: 1,023 visits since 1922, reported by the Easton Free Press in August 1924.
evidence.quote: Up to Saturday the new steel fire tower of the New Jersey Department of Conservation and Development on the summit of the Blue Mountain had been visited by 245 persons, making a total of 1023 since the tower was erected in 1922.

evidence.supports: Norman Maring employed as watchman.
evidence.quote: Norman Maring is employed as watchman to look out for forest fires in that area.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1922 papers call the summit Blue Mountain; the state's FY1923 report calls it Kittatinny Mountain. The story uses Kittatinny Mountain and notes the older name.
The July 1922 Asbury Park Press says about five miles west; the FY1923 state report says about 7 miles west. Not resolved; the story reports both.

notes_for_editor: History from 1922 to 1997 is well sourced (NHLR plus 1922-1924 press and state reports). Current status rests on NHLR visit reports from 2018 and a 2022 repainting comment, not a 2026 check. No notable fires were found in the sources read, so none are listed. The NJ DEP fire-towers page returned no text when fetched, and a Willhite lookout-history page (willhiteweb.com) appeared in search but was not read. The record's height 18.0 m matches Wikipedia's 60 ft (18 m). The record's access 'unknown' is replaced by public trail access. No photos added. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's unsupported staffing claims ('Staff came early', 'Staffing has been irregular since') were removed; the 1922-1923 staffing picture is unknown. The 'Newspapers disagreed' wording was corrected (one 1922 newspaper against the state report).
